chunk_findings.detail: In apply mode the function fails only when a step is `refused`/`unknown`, so a step left in `todo` — the same status the propose path uses to mean "not done" (`test_an_unregistered_server_is_a_todo_and_says_how`) — is treated as success. `open_` is built as the set of *all* not-done statuses `("todo", "refused", "unknown")` (line 237), and the failure message on line 239 counts exactly that set (`f"{len(open_)} step(s) not done"`), which shows the code's own notion of "not done" includes `todo`; the guard on line 238 then deliberately checks only a subset of it. Concrete input: `ddflow onboard --stage harness --apply` (or the MCP `onboard` call with `stage="harness", apply=true`) for an adopted agent whose `HS.onboard_steps(...)` leaves any step in `todo` — e.g. a step the tool cannot complete automatically, or steps skipped because an earlier step did not run. The call returns `O.ok("onboard.harness", ...)` with `data["harnesses"]` still listing unfinished steps, so the CLI exit code / MCP result reports a fully onboarded agent while onboarding is incomplete. The guard should cover every step in `open_` (i.e. `if apply and open_:`), which is also what the message's `len(open_)` assumes.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/onboard.py:237-240 (`harness()`)

chunk_findings.detail: `project_servers` now takes a `shape` argument and forwards it to `get_servers(data, shape)`, and this change also adds `import tomllib` plus `SHAPE_TOML` to the imports — but the file-reading part of the function was left as-is and still parses `mcp_rel` as JSON (`read_json(path)`, with the unchanged guard at line 54 raising `f"{mcp_rel} is not a JSON object; fix it by hand"`). Concretely: for any descriptor whose MCP config is a TOML file (`mcp_rel="config.toml"`, `shape=SHAPE_TOML`, e.g. a Codex-style `[mcp_servers.ddflow]` table), `read_json` cannot parse it, so `data` comes back as `Unreadable`, the `not isinstance(data, dict)` guard fires first, and `project_servers` raises `HarnessError("config.toml is not a JSON object; fix it by hand")` instead of returning the registered server names. `enable_project_servers(..., shape=SHAPE_TOML)` inherits the same failure, so onboarding/adopt for a non-JSON agent can neither see the registered server nor approve it — the exact "per descriptor" behaviour this change is supposed to add. The newly added `tomllib` import being unused in the function (the only place a file is parsed) is the tell that the TOML branch was dropped: the shape must drive the parser (e.g. `tomllib.loads(path.read_text())` when `shape == SHAPE_TOML`), and the "is not a JSON object" message/guard needs to match the shape.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness.py:57 (`project_servers` / `enable_project_servers`)

chunk_findings.detail: The dry-run branch re-introduces exactly the pattern the kept comment above `enable_project_servers` forbids (`enabled = data.get(enabled_key, [])`, "NOT `.get(KEY) or []`"), and then uses a substring `in` test rather than list membership. Any non-list value is either coerced to `[]` (dict/empty string/`false`) or, worse, substring-searched. Given `.claude/settings.local.json` containing `{"enabledMcpjsonServers": "ddflow"}` — a very plausible hand-edit meaning "just this one server" instead of `["ddflow"]` — `data.get(...) or []` yields the string, `"ddflow" in "ddflow"` is `True`, and `_approval` reports `approve: done` ("enabledMcpjsonServers in ..."). Even `{"enabledMcpjsonServers": "my-ddflow-servers"}` reports `done`. The same file run with `--apply` goes through `enable_project_servers`, which raises `SettingsError("... is not a list of names; not touching it")` and reports `unknown`. So the non-apply report claims the server is approved for a file the apply path explicitly refuses to touch; the status vocabulary in the docstring ("unknown (a file could not be read)") is bypassed. The value should be validated as a list of strings (or the `Unreadable`/malformed case mapped to `unknown`) before the membership test.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness.py:_approval (dry-run predicate `on = "ddflow" in (data.get(m.approve_key) or [])`)

chunk_findings.detail: In the dry-run branch the status depends only on `enabled`; `m.deny_key`/`m.approve_key + "-denied"` is only consulted inside `enable_project_servers`. With `.claude/settings.local.json` = `{"enabledMcpjsonServers": ["ddflow"], "disabledMcpjsonServers": ["ddflow"]}`, `onboard --agents claude` reports `approve: done` — but `disabledMcpjsonServers` rejects the server in every permission mode (`enable_project_servers` produces a `Refused`), and the same run with `--apply` reports `approve: refused`. Symmetrically, a file with only `disabledMcpjsonServers: ["ddflow"]` reports `todo` ("register the server first"/needs approval), i.e. an actionable step, when the step is actually impossible without the operator first editing the deny list. Since `refused` is part of the advertised status set ("the operator's own setting stands in the way"), the dry-run path should detect the deny key too; as written, `onboard` without `--apply` can never emit `refused`, so the risk the operator most needs to see is visible only after they run the mutating command.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/harness.py:_approval (deny key is never consulted when `apply=False`)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness.py:_approval (deny key is never consulted when `apply=False`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new consistency check only ties `approve_file` to `approve_key`; `deny_key` is left completely unconstrained. A descriptor can therefore set `deny_key = "disabledMcpjsonServers"` (or whatever the agent's reject list is called) while leaving both `approve_file` and `approve_key` empty, and `_validate` accepts it. Because the doc comment on the new fields states that `approve_file` is the settings file that is edited and `approve_key`/`deny_key` are lists inside it, a `deny_key` with no `approve_file` is unreachable — nothing can ever read it, so the operator's "reject this server" intent is silently dropped at load time rather than surfacing as a `DescriptorError` the way a lone `approve_key` does. Adding the same pairing requirement for `deny_key` (i.e. `if h.mcp.deny_key and not (h.mcp.approve_file and h.mcp.approve_key): raise DescriptorError(...)`) would make the misconfiguration fail loudly instead of being ignored.

chunk_findings.detail: The set of unfinished steps and the condition that decides failure disagree, and the losing side is the failure check. `open_` is built from `("todo", "refused", "unknown")` and the failure message is `f"{len(open_)} step(s) not done"`, i.e. the code itself treats a `todo` step as *not done*; but the guard is `if apply and any(s["status"] in ("refused", "unknown") for s in open_)`, which ignores `todo` entirely. Consequence: on a harness/project where a step can only be completed after `apply` has run (the change's own vocabulary for this is a step left at `todo` with instructions "how" — e.g. an agent whose MCP registration/approval cannot be performed automatically), `onboard --stage harness --apply` returns `O.ok("onboard.harness", ...)` even though the server was never registered/approved and the ladder level advertised via `best_level(h)` was not actually installed. A caller coordinating with the onboard-prompt/adopt flow (`apply=True` is the signal for "installed", and the same function returns `O.failed` precisely to stop that flow) will treat the agent as onboarded and stop retrying, leaving the user running the agent without the ddflow MCP server. The companion inconsistency is visible one line up: when a refusal *does* trigger the failure branch, the count in the message is `len(open_)`, so it also reports the ignored `todo` steps ("1 refused + 2 todo" → "3 step(s) not done"), confirming that the intended predicate over `open_` was the whole list, not the `refused`/`unknown` subset.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/onboard.py:237-239 (in `harness()`)

chunk_findings.detail: `project_servers` now takes a `shape` argument and forwards it to `get_servers`, and this same module adds `from .adopt import ... SHAPE_TOML ...` plus `import tomllib` — i.e. the change advertises that a descriptor may read its server list from a TOML-shaped project file. But the parse step above line 57 is untouched: it still calls `read_json(...)`, and the guard it raises is literally `HarnessError(f"{mcp_rel} is not a JSON object; fix it by hand")`. `get_servers` operates on already-parsed data, so the shape cannot rescue the parse. Given a descriptor whose project MCP config is TOML (e.g. a codex-style `config.toml` holding `[mcp_servers.ddflow]`), `read_json` cannot `json.loads` that text, returns `Unreadable`, and line 55 raises `HarnessError("... could not be read (...); fix it by hand")`. So the one non-default shape this module imports, `SHAPE_TOML`, is unusable: `onboard`/`adopt` for such an agent reports a hard error (or a bogus "unregistered server is a todo") even when the server is correctly registered, and `enable_project_servers`, which threads the descriptor's `shape` straight into this reader, approves nothing. The new `tomllib` import is not used to branch the read here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harness.py:57 (project_servers)

chunk_findings.detail: `_approval` decides the reported approval status by membership-testing `"ddflow"` directly into whatever `data.get(m.approve_key)` holds, without the list-type guard that `enable_project_servers` (whose own comment three screens up states the rule: `.get(KEY, [])`, NOT `.get(KEY) or []`) applies to the very same key. A valid-JSON settings file whose `approve_key` is a non-list is therefore mis-reported. Given an approval file containing `{"enabledMcpjsonServers": {"ddflow": false}}` (a botched merge, or an operator who nested the name), `data.get(...)` is a truthy dict and `"ddflow" in {...}` is `True`, so `onboard_steps`/`_approval` emit `_step("approve", "done", ...)` — the report tells the operator the server is approved, while the actual apply path (`enable_project_servers`) would raise `SettingsError("... is not a list of names; not touching it")` and leave the file untouched. The same happens with a string value: `{"enabledMcpjsonServers": "ddflow-disabled"}` matches by substring and is reported `done`. This contradicts the function's own contract ("A step is never `done` on a guess") and hides the malformed key that the type check exists to surface; the falsy half of the same `or []` masks malformed values the other way (`{"...": ""}` is silently reported `todo` instead of `unknown`). The read path should type-check the value as a list of names and return `unknown` otherwise, the way `enable_project_servers` refuses to touch it.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/harness.py` — `_approval`, the `"ddflow" in (data.get(m.approve_key) or [])` read path

chunk_findings.detail: The new pairing guard only covers `approve_file`/`approve_key`; it does not cover `deny_key`, even though all three fields describe the same settings file (per the comment above the fields, "the repo-relative settings file, the list that approves a server and the list that rejects one"). A descriptor that sets only `deny_key = "disabledMcpjsonServers"` with `approve_file = ""` and `approve_key = ""` passes `_validate` cleanly, yet there is no file to write the deny list into. So the invariant the change is trying to enforce ("these fields go together / all empty means none") is incomplete: a malformed descriptor that names a deny key but no approval target loads without error, and the deny list is either written to an empty/derived path or silently dropped downstream (whichever the `services/harness.py` code does), instead of being rejected at load time like the symmetric `approve_file`-without-`approve_key` case is. The check should treat `deny_key` as also requiring `approve_file`/`approve_key`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/harnessreg.py:273 (`_validate`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `apply` property description was left as "Act on the proposal (preflight/legacy/memory)" while this same change adds `harness` as a stage that the tool description says performs "register, approve, hooks, best ladder level" — i.e. actions that only happen when `apply=true`. Given `stage=harness`, a caller (this tool is consumed by a model, so the property text is the contract) reads that `apply` is meaningful only for preflight/legacy/memory and can omit `apply=true`, in which case the harness stage returns the proposal and never registers/approves/installs hooks. The stage list was updated but the apply list was not, so the schema now contradicts the documented behavior of the newly added stage.
